regional.headline: Lujo virus. Nosocomial haemorrhagic fever outbreak in southern Africa.
regional.geography: Lujo virus. Nosocomial haemorrhagic fever outbreak in southern Africa.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Abrupt fever, profound weakness, myalgia, then vomiting and high-volume diarrhoea with electrolyte derangement, shock and sometimes haemorrhage. Survivors experience uveitis, arthralgia and neurological sequelae; virus persists in semen, aqueous humour and CSF, enabling late sexual transmission and relapse.
regional.headline: Filovirus causing Ebola disease, with case fatality historically 25–90%; now treatable with monoclonal antibodies and preventable by vaccination.
regional.prevention: The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) used in ring vaccination, plus the Ad26/MVA regimen; safe burial practices and infection prevention and control.
regional.geography: Central and West Africa — the 2013–2016 West African epidemic caused over 28,000 cases.
regional.evidence_note: Virus, viral RNA or specific antibody found in the reservoir host or in livestock, with no human case reported. The virus is present in the country; whether it has ever infected a person there is unknown.

regional.syndrome: Haemorrhagic fever clinically similar to Ebola disease.
regional.headline: The first filovirus recognised (Marburg, 1967), with case fatality in outbreaks of 24–88%; no licensed vaccine or therapeutic.
regional.prevention: Avoid bat-inhabited mines and caves; strict IPC and safe burial.
regional.geography: Angola, DRC, Uganda, Kenya, Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda, Ghana.
regional.evidence_note: Virus, viral RNA or specific antibody found in the reservoir host or in livestock, with no human case reported. The virus is present in the country; whether it has ever infected a person there is unknown.

regional.incubation: 1–9 days after tick bite; 5–13 days after blood contact.
regional.syndrome: Abrupt fever, myalgia, severe headache, then haemorrhagic manifestations, hepatic dysfunction and DIC. Case fatality ranges from 5% to 40%. Nosocomial outbreaks among healthcare workers are a defining feature.
regional.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.
regional.prevention: Tick protection, safe slaughter practice, and strict barrier nursing with full PPE. No licensed vaccine (a Bulgarian inactivated vaccine has limited use).
regional.geography: Africa, the Balkans, Middle East, Central and South Asia, western China; expanding with Hyalomma range into Spain and southern Europe.
regional.evidence_note: Virus, viral RNA or specific antibody found in the reservoir host or in livestock, with no human case reported. The virus is present in the country; whether it has ever infected a person there is unknown.

vectors: Aedes mcintoshi (and other floodwater Aedes, with transovarial maintenance)
regional.syndrome: Most human infections are a self-limiting febrile illness. Complications: retinitis with permanent visual loss (1–10%), meningoencephalitis, and haemorrhagic fever with hepatic failure (<1%, but ~50% fatal).
regional.headline: Zoonotic phlebovirus causing devastating ruminant abortion storms and human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen.
regional.prevention: Livestock vaccination, movement controls, protective equipment during slaughter, vector control. No licensed human vaccine.
regional.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa, Madagascar, Egypt, Arabian peninsula; outbreaks follow heavy rainfall and flooding.
regional.evidence_note: Virus, viral RNA or specific antibody found in the reservoir host or in livestock, with no human case reported. The virus is present in the country; whether it has ever infected a person there is unknown.
